# CHAPTER XIV:

DILETTANTISM (1865-1866)

The campaign of 1864 and Lincoln's reëlection set the American Minister on so firm a footing that the private secretary's own anxieties were over. With his father's term ending, he might look forward to going home in 1865. The time for going into the army had passed; the son knew he was doing himself no good by staying in London, but thus far in life he had done himself no good anywhere, and reached his twenty-seventh birthday without having advanced a step that he could see beyond his twenty-first.

The London climate told on the family, and the physicians prescribed a winter in Italy. The private secretary was detached as their escort — a form of travel hitherto untried, in all possible luxury, at someone else's expense. The Cornice in vettura was delightful; Sorrento in winter offered hills and grottoes; Rome at Easter was an experience necessary for the education of every properly trained private secretary. The assassination of President Lincoln fell on the party while they were at Rome, where it seemed singularly fitting to that nursery of murderers and murdered, as though America were also getting educated. Again one went to meditate on the steps of the Santa Maria in Ara Cœli, but the lesson seemed as shallow as before. Nothing happened.

When he sat down again at his desk in Portland Place before a mass of copy in arrears, he saw before him a world so changed as to be beyond connection with the past. His identity, if one could call a bundle of disconnected memories an identity, seemed to remain; but his life was once more broken into separate pieces; he was a spider and had to spin a new web in some new place with a new attachment.

All his American friends and contemporaries who were still alive looked singularly commonplace without uniforms, and hastened to get married and retire into back streets and suburbs until they could find employment. Minister Adams was going home "next fall," and when the fall came, "next spring," and when spring came, President Johnson was at loggerheads with the Senate, and it was best to keep things unchanged. The members of the Legation continued the daily routine of English society, which, after becoming a habit, threatened to become a vice. Evidently he must set to work; he must get a new education; he must begin a career of his own.

Nothing was easier to say, but even his father admitted two careers closed. For the law, diplomacy had unfitted him; for diplomacy he already knew too much. One profession alone seemed possible — the press. It was an inferior pulpit; an anonymous schoolmaster; a cheap boarding-school; but it was still the nearest approach to a career for the literary survivor of a wrecked education. Since he could not go home for practical training, he set to work to do what he could in London.

The path that led somewhere was the English habit of mind, which deepened its ruts every day. The English mind was like the London drawing-room, a comfortable and easy spot, filled with bits and fragments of incoherent furnitures, which were never meant to go together, and could be arranged in any relation without making a whole, except by the square room. Most young Englishmen drifted to the race-course or the moors; a few towards books; a number took to what, for want of a better name, they called Art. Of all supposed English tastes, that of art was the most alluring and treacherous. Once drawn into it, one had small chance of escape, for it had no centre or circumference, no beginning, middle, or end, no origin, no object, and no conceivable result as education.

In Yorkshire he met Frank Palgrave, whose ferocious art criticism had made the *Saturday Review* a terror, and whose "Golden Treasury" had taught Adams more literary education than he ever got from any taste of his own. Through Palgrave came Woolner, sculptor and savage critic, who took British want-of-art seriously, almost ferociously, as a personal grievance, in language much like Carlyle's. Adams went to the sales and bought what he was told to buy — now a classical drawing called Rafael, now a water-color by Girtin or Cotman — and watched the experts of the British Museum contradict each other and themselves on every authentication. He once paid twelve shillings for a drawing supposed to be Rafael, and kept it on his mantelpiece for forty years to see whether any critic or artist would ever stop to look at it. None ever did. Art was a superb field for education, but at every turn he met the same old figure, like a battered and illegible signpost that ought to direct him to the next station but never did. There was no next station.

Turning from British art to British literature, one met the same dangers. The historical school was a playground of traps and pitfalls; fatally one fell into the sink of history — antiquarianism. Macaulay was the English historian, and any one who should even distantly imitate Macaulay would perish in self-contempt. When Dr. Palfrey, busy with his "History of New England," suggested an article on Captain John Smith's relations with Pocahontas as a likely stone for a beginner to throw, Adams could suggest nothing better. He planted himself in the British Museum, patiently worked over the material for three or four months, and the article appeared in the *North American Review* in January, 1867.

Surely, here was something to ponder, as a step in education. In spite of personal wishes, intentions, and prejudices; in spite of civil wars and diplomatic education; in spite of determination to be actual, daily, and practical, Henry Adams found himself, at twenty-eight, still in English society, dragged on one side into English dilettantism, which of all dilettantism he held the most futile; and, on the other, into American antiquarianism, which of all antiquarianism he held the most foolish. This was the result of five years in London. Even then he knew it to be a false start. He had wholly lost his way. If he were ever to amount to anything, he must begin a new education, in a new place, with a new purpose.
